title: Coordination Compounds
summary: A coordination compound has a central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ligands (ions or molecules which donate electron pairs) by coordinate bonds. In [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 the coordination sphere is [Co(NH3)6]^3+ (the complex ion) and the counter ions are Cl−. Coordination number is the number of ligand donor atoms attached to the metal (6 in [Co(NH3)6]^3+, 4 in [Ni(CN)4]^2−). Ligands: monodentate (Cl−, NH3, H2O, CN−), bidentate (ethylenediamine en, oxalate ox^2−), polydentate (EDTA, hexadentate) and ambidentate (NO2−/ONO−, SCN−/NCS−, which can bind through two different atoms). Werner's theory: metals have primary valence (oxidation state, ionisable) and secondary valence (coordination number, non-ionisable, directional). Charge on complex = sum of the metal's oxidation state and ligand charges. Double salts break into simple ions in water whereas complexes keep the coordination sphere.

IUPAC naming: ligands first in alphabetical order, then the metal; the cation is named before the anion; prefixes di, tri for simple ligands and bis, tris for complex ligands; the oxidation state of the metal in Roman numerals; for anionic complexes the metal ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, platinate, cobaltate). Anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, oxalato); neutral ligands keep their names (ammine, aqua, carbonyl, ethane-1,2-diamine). Examples: [PtCl6]^2− hexachloridoplatinate(IV); K[Ag(CN)2] potassium dicyanidoargentate(I); [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. Structural isomerism: ionisation ([Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br), hydrate, linkage ([Co(NH3)5NO2]^2+ nitro and [Co(NH3)5ONO]^2+ nitrito), coordination ([Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]). Stereoisomerism: geometrical (cis/trans in square planar [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] and octahedral [CoCl2(en)2]+, which has cis and trans forms; the cis form is optically active, giving 3 stereoisomers in all; fac/mer in MA3B3) and optical isomerism (non-superimposable mirror images, e.g. [Co(en)3]^3+).
## Bonding: VBT and crystal field theory

VBT: ligands donate pairs to empty hybrid orbitals of the metal – octahedral d²sp³ (inner orbital, low spin, uses (n−1)d: [Fe(CN)6]^3−, [Co(NH3)6]^3+) or sp³d² (outer orbital, high spin, uses nd: [FeF6]^3−, [CoF6]^3−); tetrahedral sp³ ([NiCl4]^2−, paramagnetic); square planar dsp² ([Ni(CN)4]^2−, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], diamagnetic). [Fe(CN)6]^3− has one unpaired electron (paramagnetic, μ ≈ 1.73 BM). Crystal field theory: ligands split the d orbitals; in octahedral complexes into t2g (lower) and eg (higher) with splitting Δo; strong field ligands (CN−, CO) give low spin, weak field ligands (I−, Br−, Cl−, F−, H2O) give high spin. Colour arises from d–d transitions: [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ is green while [Ni(CN)4]^2− is colourless (square planar d⁸, strong field, diamagnetic and its absorption is not in the visible region). Applications: EDTA in water softening, cis-platin in cancer therapy, extraction of Ag and Au by cyanide complexes, chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe), vitamin B12 (Co).

April 2025
What is meant by linkage isomerism? Give an example.
Isomerism due to ambidentate ligands that can attach through different donor atoms. [Co(NH3)5NO2]^2+ (N-bonded nitro) and [Co(NH3)5ONO]^2+ (O-bonded nitrito).
October 2025
What are outer-orbital and inner-orbital complexes? Give an example of each.
Outer-orbital: octahedral complex using sp³d² (nd orbitals), high spin, e.g. [FeF6]^3−. Inner-orbital: uses d²sp³ ((n−1)d orbitals), low spin, e.g. [Fe(CN)6]^3−.
October 2025
Why is a solution of [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ green while [Ni(CN)4]^2− is colourless?

In [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ (Ni^2+, d⁸) two unpaired electrons undergo d–d transitions absorbing visible light. In [Ni(CN)4]^2− the strong-field CN− pairs all electrons (dsp², square planar, diamagnetic), so there is no d–d absorption in the visible region.
April 2025
Why is [Fe(CN)6]^3− paramagnetic?
Fe^3+ is d⁵; with strong CN− ligands the electrons pair up to d²sp³, leaving one unpaired electron.
April 2026
What is a chelate? Give an example.
A complex in which a polydentate ligand binds the metal through two or more donor atoms forming a ring, such as [Co(en)3]^3+ or the EDTA complex of Ca^2+.
Define coordination number and give an example.
The number of donor atoms bonded to the central metal in a complex; it is 6 in [Co(NH3)6]^3+.
Name the complex [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 and state its coordination number.
Pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride; coordination number 6.
sa: For the complex [CoCl2(en)2]+: (a) how many geometrical isomers exist? (b) Is optical isomerism possible?

(a) Two geometrical isomers: cis (Cl groups adjacent) and trans (Cl groups opposite).
(b) The cis form lacks a plane of symmetry and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (d and l); the trans form is optically inactive. So three stereoisomers exist.
Write the isomers of [Co(NH3)6][Cr(C2O4)3] and the type of isomerism shown.
[Cr(NH3)6][Co(C2O4)3] is the isomer, formed by exchange of the metals between cation and anion. This is coordination isomerism.
Explain the bonding in [Fe(CN)6]^4− and [FeF6]^3− on the basis of valence bond theory.

[Fe(CN)6]^4−: Fe^2+ is d⁶; strong CN− pairs the electrons, using two 3d, one 4s and three 4p orbitals (d²sp³), diamagnetic, inner orbital. [FeF6]^3−: Fe^3+ d⁵; weak F− does not pair them, using 4s, 4p and two 4d (sp³d²), five unpaired electrons, outer orbital, paramagnetic.
Explain crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes and the difference between high spin and low spin.

In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into t2g (lower) and eg (higher). If Δo is greater than the pairing energy (strong-field ligand), electrons pair up in t2g (low spin); if Δo is smaller (weak-field ligand), electrons occupy eg before pairing (high spin).
Write the IUPAC names and the oxidation states of the metals in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl, K4[Fe(CN)6] and [Ni(CO)4].
State three applications of coordination compounds.

EDTA is used to estimate Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ (hardness) and in lead poisoning; cis-platin is an anticancer drug; extraction of silver and gold by cyanide complexes; haemoglobin, chlorophyll and vitamin B12 are coordination compounds.
la: (a) Give the IUPAC names of (i) [PtCl6]^2− (ii) K[Ag(CN)2]. (b) For [CoCl2(en)2]+ (i) identify the number of geometrical isomers and draw their structures; (ii) state whether optical isomers exist.

(a) (i) Hexachloridoplatinate(IV); (ii) potassium dicyanidoargentate(I).
(b) (i) Two: cis – the two Cl on adjacent corners of the octahedron with the two en rings spanning the remaining positions; trans – the two Cl on opposite corners (axial) with both en rings in the plane. (ii) The cis isomer has no plane of symmetry and shows optical isomerism (d and l forms); the trans isomer is optically inactive.
(a) Write the isomers of [Co(NH3)6][Cr(C2O4)3] and name the type of isomerism. (b) A solution of [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ is green but a solution of [Ni(CN)4]^2− is colourless. Explain (Ni = 28).

(a) [Cr(NH3)6][Co(C2O4)3]; coordination isomerism (the ligands are distributed differently between the cationic and anionic parts).
(b) Ni^2+ is 3d⁸. In [Ni(H2O)6]^2+, H2O is a weak ligand, so two unpaired electrons remain, sp³d² (outer), and d–d transitions give green colour. In [Ni(CN)4]^2−, CN− is a strong ligand which pairs the electrons, dsp² square planar, diamagnetic – no d–d transition in the visible region, hence colourless.
(a) Explain Werner's theory. (b) Name the types of isomerism in coordination compounds with one example of each.

(a) Metals show two types of valence: primary (ionisable, equal to the oxidation state) and secondary (non-ionisable, equal to coordination number, directed in space to give geometry such as octahedral); e.g. CoCl3·6NH3 has 3 primary and 6 secondary valences and gives 3 Cl− with AgNO3.
(b) Ionisation – [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br; hydrate – [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 and [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O; linkage – nitro and nitrito; coordination – [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]; geometrical – cis/trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]; optical – [Co(en)3]^3+.
(a) Explain the geometry and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)4]^2−, [NiCl4]^2− and [Fe(CN)6]^3− using VBT. (b) State two biological importances of complexes.

(a) [Ni(CN)4]^2−: Ni^2+ d⁸, strong ligand pairs electrons, dsp², square planar, diamagnetic. [NiCl4]^2−: weak ligand, sp³, tetrahedral, two unpaired electrons, paramagnetic. [Fe(CN)6]^3−: Fe^3+ d⁵ with CN−, d²sp³, octahedral, one unpaired electron, paramagnetic.
(b) Chlorophyll (Mg) in photosynthesis and haemoglobin (Fe) in oxygen transport.
